_about: Every field a production eval dataset row can carry. Reference for Topic 9.

_legend.supported: true = eval.py in this folder already reads it; false = not implemented yet
_legend.used_by: code = affects your score | human = documentation only
_legend.priority: start = use from day one | soon = add when it hurts | later = advanced

_start_here._note: 7 fields. Do not add more until a real problem demands it.
_start_here.input: Don't cancel my order - I just want to know where it is. It's #111
_start_here.why: Policy: act on final intent, not on earlier words.

_trap: Unknown fields are silently ignored. Writing 'expected_arguments' instead of 'expected_args' produces a FAKE FAILURE on a perfectly correct answer. Always check which names your harness actually reads.

groups.purpose: Name the test and control whether it runs.

fields.description: The test's permanent name. You will cite it in tickets for months.
fields.note: Never renumber. Renaming an id destroys your failure history.

fields.description: dev = rows you tune prompts against. holdout = rows you touch rarely, to check you did not just memorise the dev set.
fields.note: Add this the day you start editing prompts to fix eval failures.

fields.description: Turn a row off without deleting it.
Known unreliable row. Still runs and is reported, but is not allowed to fail the build.
This row is expected to fail today. Alerts you when it starts PASSING, so you notice the fix.
Who to ask when someone disputes this label.
When the row was written. Old rows go stale as the product changes.

groups.purpose: What the system under test receives. This is the ONLY part sent to the model.

fields.description: The customer's message, exactly as a real user would type it, typos included.
fields.note: Do not clean it up. Cleaned inputs give you a cleaned-up score.

fields.description: A whole conversation instead of one line. Needed the moment behavior depends on earlier turns.
Documents retrieved and handed to the model. Required for RAG evals: you cannot judge groundedness without knowing what it was given.
The starting state of the world: which orders exist, their status. Without it, 'cancel #123' has no defined correct answer.
Who is asking. Correct behavior often depends on tier, locale, or permissions.
Image, audio, or file inputs for multimodal systems.

groups.purpose: What the agent should DO. The most important group for agents.

fields.description: Which tool should be called. null means 'call nothing, reply in words'.
fields.note: Rows with null are your negative cases. Without them, an agent that always calls a tool scores well.

fields.description: The argument values the tool should be called with.
fields.note: Only graded when expected_tool matched. Args checked against the wrong tool are a meaningless number.

fields.description: How strictly to compare each argument. exact = character-for-character. fuzzy = words mostly overlap (for free text like addresses). ignore = do not check.
An ORDERED sequence of calls, for agents that take several steps.
Any one of these is acceptable. Use when two tools are genuinely both correct, instead of forcing a fake single answer.
Must NEVER be called on this input. Your safety rail.
fields.note: Worth far more than text checks. A wrong word is embarrassing; a wrong action costs money.

fields.description: Call budget. Catches agents stuck in a loop.
Side effects that must not happen, described as behavior rather than text. Graded by inspecting the tool calls, not the reply.

groups.purpose: What the agent should SAY. This is all you have on rows where expected_tool is null.

fields.description: Every one of these must appear in the reply (case-insensitive).
None of these may appear. Catches catastrophes cheaply.
fields.note: On a row that must do nothing, the reply saying 'cancelled' means the agent thinks it acted.

fields.description: Pattern the reply must match. Good for formats: dates, ids, currency.
A reference answer. Cannot be compared with ==; needs fuzzy matching, embeddings, or an LLM judge.
fields.example: Your refund for order 321 was processed on Tuesday.

fields.description: Several valid answers. Honest about questions with more than one right response.
example: That is outside what I can do.

fields.description: Which sources the answer must cite. A right answer citing the wrong document is still a failure.
The agent must decline. Distinguishes 'I cannot' from 'I will not'.
For structured output: the reply must validate against this schema.

groups.purpose: How this specific row gets scored. Different rows deserve different graders.

fields.description: Who decides pass or fail for this row.
Written scoring guide handed to a judge. Vague rubrics produce random scores.
fields.example: Pass if the reply asks for the order id and does not claim any action was taken.

fields.description: Pin the judge model. Changing the judge changes every score, so it must be recorded.
Pass mark when scoring is a scale rather than pass/fail.
How much this row counts. A wrongly cancelled order should outweigh a clumsy greeting.
fields.note: Unweighted averages quietly say every mistake costs the same. They never do.

fields.description: Allow 0.5 rather than only 0 or 1. Useful when 'right tool, wrong id' is better than 'wrong tool'.

groups.purpose: How results get grouped. The group that earns its keep: 87% overall hid address 0%.

fields.description: Free-form slice labels. A row can carry several.
fields.note: The single highest-value field after expected_tool. No tags means no diagnosis.

fields.description: One primary bucket per row, unlike tags. Keeps the report readable as the dataset grows.
Track the hard slice separately, or easy rows will mask real regressions.
How bad failure is here. Lets you gate releases on safety failures while tolerating cosmetic ones.
Non-English performance hides inside a global average. Slice it out.
Failures do not cost the same across segments.

groups.purpose: Where the label came from and who is accountable for it. Boring until an auditor asks.

fields.description: Where this test case came from.
fields.note: If most rows are 'handwritten', you are testing your imagination, not your users.

fields.description: The policy line that makes this label correct. Written for the version of you that reads it in three months.
fields.example: Policy: act on final intent, not on earlier words.
fields.note: If you cannot write this, the row is too ambiguous to keep. This is the cheapest quality filter you have.

fields.description: Link back to the real production trace this row came from, so you can see the full context later.
Which human decided the expected answer.
Flags rows annotators argued about. If humans disagree, an LLM judge has no chance.
Second pair of eyes on the label. Audit trail.
Pointer to the document and section this label comes from.
Real customer data. Must be scrubbed before the dataset is shared or sent to a third-party judge.
The bug or ticket this row was born from. These are your most valuable rows: real failures that already happened once.

groups.purpose: Correctness is not the only requirement. A right answer in 40 seconds is a wrong answer.

fields.description: Fail the row if the response took longer than this.
Fail if the row cost too much to answer.
Catches runaway generation and rambling replies.
Per-row timeout override, for rows you know are slow.

_add_next_in_this_order: split - the day you start tuning prompts against the dataset
severity + weight - so a wrongly cancelled order outranks a typo
forbidden_tools + must_not - side effects cost real money
expected_tools - when the agent takes more than one step
grader + rubric - when == stops working and you need a judge
